# The spans Find is documented to have ignored: a span reaching outside the
# text, and a span whose Start is not less than its End.
#
# The patterns here report the spans they are built with whatever text they are
# handed, which is the only way to state a rule about a span a pattern must not
# be trusted with. A case here hands a text of six bytes to the span beside it
# unless its name says otherwise, and two of them do: one hands a longer text
# to a span reaching past six, and one hands an empty text to a span over the
# whole of it. None of these cases is held to what follows a value around:
# nothing moves for these patterns when the text around a value grows, because
# they never look at it.

spans:    reported

patterns: span-empty

case:     an empty span is ignored
in:       abcdef
out:      abcdef

patterns: span-reversed

case:     a span whose start is past its end is ignored
in:       abcdef
out:      abcdef

patterns: span-negative

case:     a span starting before the text is ignored
in:       abcdef
out:      abcdef

patterns: span-past-the-end

case:     a span reaching past the text is ignored
in:       abcdef
out:      abcdef

case:     the same span in a text long enough to hold it is used
in:       abcdefgh
out:      abcd«past-the-end»h

patterns: span-unusable-beside-a-value

case:     an unusable span leaves the usable ones alone
in:       abcdef
out:      «mixed»cdef

patterns: span-unordered

case:     spans reported out of order are sorted
in:       abcdef
out:      «unordered»cd«unordered»

patterns: span-duplicated

case:     the same span reported twice is redacted once
in:       abcdef
out:      «duplicated»cdef

patterns: span-whole-input

case:     a span over the whole text
in:       abcdef
out:      «whole»

case:     a span over the whole text of an empty text is ignored
in:
out:

patterns: span-inside-a-rune

# Both ends of a span must fall on a rune boundary, and the built-in patterns
# and Regexp cannot report one that does not — every built-in decides its ends
# on an ASCII alphabet, and Go's regexp matches runes. This is the one shape
# Pattern.Find documents as a demand on a Find written by hand rather than as
# a possibility any pattern above can reach: neither ignored nor repaired, so
# the bytes either side of it are written back as they were found and what is
# left of the rune stands beside the mark. "日本" is two three-byte runes, and
# the span here cuts the first of them after its lead byte.

case:     a span cutting a rune in half is used as it is
in:       日本
out:      «half»\x97\xa5本
